answer:
This name is read inside-out as a genealogy: each bracket pair tells you who modified whom. Let me confirm it exists on the open program:

Confirmed — the four vertical inner walls carry exactly this shape of name. Reading it inside-out:

**`shell/inner[…body/side[base.outline.bottom]…]`**

- **`base.outline.bottom`** — the deepest ancestor: sketch `base`, rectangle `outline`, its `bottom` side edge (`.rect` names its sides `bottom/right/top/left`). Extruding that edge is what created the face.
- **`body/side[…]`** — the extrude feature `body` turned that sketch line into a side wall, so the face is named `body/side` and records the sketch edge it came from in brackets.
- **`shell/inner[…]`** — the `shell` feature hollowed the box, offsetting each outer wall inward to make the 2 mm wall. The offset copy keeps the parent's name and wraps it: `shell/inner` = the inner wall produced from `body/side[…]`.

So the rule is `<feature>/<role>[<parent face name>]`, applied recursively. The brackets are provenance, not just labels: even when a later feature splits or offsets a face (a `#a`/`#b` suffix appears then), the name still says exactly which sketch line the wall descends from. That's why the name survives edits — change the rectangle size in `base` and the face is still `shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`, so selectors like `j.sel.names('faces', ['shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]'])` keep resolving.

Compare the fifth face returned: `shell/inner[body/start]` — the floor's inner face descends from `body`'s start face (the original sketch plane face), which has no deeper bracket because a plane face isn't traced to a single sketch entity. You can inspect any chain with `why('shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]')` or [select it](lab:face?name=shell%2Finner%5Bbody%2Fside%5Bbase.outline.bottom%5D%5D).

- The failing boundary is real, not a fluke: 2.4, 2.6 and 2.8 mm all compile cleanly; exactly 3 mm does not.

Why: the base sketch's rectangle has 3 mm corner rounds (that's why the box has 19 faces, not 12 — each corner adds a cylindrical face to the shell's inner surface). When the shell offsets the walls inward by the wall thickness, the inner corner radius is $r_{outer} - wall$. At wall = 2.8 mm the inner corner still has a 0.2 mm radius; at wall = 3 mm the inner corner radius hits **exactly zero** — the offset surface degenerates, and the B-rep kernel refuses to build it.

So a 3 mm wall can't be had on this box as drawn. Two ways forward if you want it: reduce the outer corner radius (e.g. `r: 4` gives a 1 mm inner corner at wall 3), or drop the rounds entirely. Note the shell thickness and the sketch fillet now genuinely depend on each other — worth keeping in mind for any future wall changes. If you'd like, I can make the sketch radius an expression like `r = wall + 1 mm` so it always clears.

It's printed on its side, along **−Y**: bbox on the bed 35 × 18 mm, only 12 mm tall, 60 layers.

The orientation decision is lexicographic — least support first, then most bed contact, then least height (the decision is visible at `cable-clip` in the trace):

- **±Y (side down): 0 mm³ of support.** The clip's profile is extruded straight through, so lying on its side every surface is either vertical or the flat profile face — nothing overhangs.
- **±Z (top/bottom of the clip down): 1451–1510 mm³ of support.** That's the jaw's underside and the cable channel facing up — the worst choice, as you'd expect for a jaw that grips over the desk edge.
- **±X: 134–1638 mm³**, and −X (the mouth down) needs a lot; the tie-break also favours ±Y's clean flat bed contact (240 mm² of the side face).

−Y beats +Y only on the last tie-break (height 12.0 both ways; the compiler lists +Y as "next"), so the printed result is identical in practice — the "next:" note in the reason says so. No supports, no brim drama; `supportVolume: 0` and the overhang list is empty.

One thing to check with a real print: the mouth's lead-in on the underside prints as-is on the side face, which is fine, but if you ever add a chamfer or lip there, re-check that the −Y choice survives — I can re-run the comparison after any outline change if you'd like.

answer:
One full turn moves the rack **113.097 mm** — the pinion's pitch circumference.

- Pitch radius $r = \tfrac{m z}{2} = \tfrac{2 \times 18}{2} = 18\ \text{mm}$ (that's the `pitchLineDistance` [j.inspect.gearMesh](lab:show?view=code) reports, and the same number the base's `axle` port sits at).
- Travel per turn $= 2\pi r = 2\pi \cdot 18 = 113.097\ \text{mm}$, which `mesh.travelPerTurn` confirms directly.

Note the coupling rule in your notes: travel = $r \cdot \theta$, so a quarter turn is 28.27 mm, and conversely moving the rack 100 mm (nearly the full 100.5 mm rack length, $16\pi\cdot2$) needs the pinion turned by $100/18\ \text{rad} = 318.3°$. Also worth knowing: the rack's total travel before running off the mesh is only about 100.5 mm minus the meshing overlap, so a full turn slightly outruns the 16-tooth rack.

answer:
The hinge uses the **`printInPlace` fit class, with a gap of 0.40 mm per side** — so the Ø3 mm pin is modelled at `j.fit.pin(3 mm, 'printInPlace')` = $3 - 2 \times 0.4 = 2.2$ mm, and each knuckle bore at $3 + 2 \times 0.4 + 0.1 = 3.9$ mm. The script sets it explicitly at [script.js line 15–16](lab:open?file=script.js&line=15): `clearance: 'printInPlace'` on `j.lib.hinge.pin`, and the local `c = 0.4` stand-off between halves matches the class (line 12), so the two bodies never come closer than the clearance.

As for calibration: **no**. Every `gap.*` param carries the provenance `default fit classes (uncalibrated)` — these are the shipped defaults (press 0.05, snug 0.10, slide 0.20, free 0.30, printInPlace 0.40 mm per side) for a generic printer, not values measured on your machine. The compile raises no `fit.uncalibrated` info here (the hinge library seems to absorb it), but the param source says it plainly.

If you want real numbers for your printer, the path is a test coupon: `j.fit.coupon({ kind: 'pin-hole', steps: 10 })` prints a graded set of pin/hole pairs, you note which gaps actually turn freely, then `j.fit.calibrate(rows)` fits `actual = a·nominal + b` and produces calibrated classes you can pass to `j.fit.profile('mk4-petg', { classes: {...} })`. Until then, 0.4 mm/side is a conservative PLA default — usually fine for a 3 mm hinge pin, but a coupon would tell you whether you could tighten to ~0.3 mm for a less sloppy swing.

The front view (the sketch plane, XZ) shows it clearly. The outline is a single closed **C-shaped spring clamp**, 18 mm tall across the desk, 35 mm from the spine to the jaw tips, with a hook folded back underneath. Walking the outline:

- **The spine** — the tall vertical wall on the left, 3 mm thick ($t$). It's the flexible leaf of the spring: as printed, its layers run along its length, so it bends without delaminating.
- **The top jaw** — runs right from the spine over the desk's top face, ending in a **grip bump** that steps down by `grip` (0.6 mm) and a 1 mm lead-in chamfer, so the clip pushes on and the bump pinches the board's top face.
- **The bottom jaw** — mirrors this under the desk: a horizontal arm at the desk's underside with a matching upward grip bump and lead-in. Together the two bumps clamp an 18 mm board with $2 \times 0.6$ mm of interference, inside the 0.4–0.8 mm fit rule.
- **The hook below** — from the bottom jaw the outline folds back down and under itself: down the back, a horizontal **cable channel** 8 mm wide (`cable`), then a lip that rises and closes over it, leaving an opening on the right. That's the push-on capture for the cable(s) hanging under the desk edge.

Everything is written as expressions of the five params (`desk`, `cable`, `t`, `jaw`, `grip`) in the `outline` polyline in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=6) — change `desk` and both jaws and the spine move together. The current values sit right on the brief's rules: $t = 3$ mm walls (≥ 2 mm) and 0.6 mm grip.

**What's in it**
- `script.js` builds the cat head as a Ø `across / 2` circle extruded to `t` (4 mm), with two triangular ear triangles joined to it. All ear coordinates are expressions over `across` (base points at `0.96 · across/2` on the circle, tips at `1.45 · across/2`), so any config or slider reshape the whole cat — no hardcoded sizes.
- The magnet pocket is modelled as a **cut from the solid** via `j.lib.magnet({ d: 'magnet_d', h: 'magnet_h' })` with `op: 'cut'`, placed with a frame whose z points into the material (`z: j.dir('-Z')`) at the back face. That gives a press-fit pocket Ø10.2 mm (10 mm + 2 × 0.05 mm press gap), 2.2 mm deep, floor at z = 2.2 mm — leaving ≈ 1.8 mm of material (`back = t − magnet_h`) in front of the magnet, so it does **not** go through.
- Layouts live in `.configs` (`small` 24 mm, `standard` 30 mm, `large` 36 mm), not in edited params, per the rule; `across` and `t` are exposed as sliders. No fillets anywhere — the bed edge stays sharp.

- Compiles clean: 1 body, 3 features, 2 sketches, 0 DOF, 10 faces, no errors or warnings.

answer:
That name is genealogy, read right to left — each composable step records the thing it came from.

**The innermost part, `base.outline.bottom`**, is a sketch entity. The sketch [base](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22) is `.rect('outline', 'w', 'd', { center: true, r: 'r' })`, and a `.rect` names its four sides `outline.bottom right top left` plus its corner arcs `outline.bl br tr tl`. So `bottom` is the straight side of the rectangle at $y=-20$ (it runs from $[-27,-20]$ to $[27,-20]$, i.e. $54 = w - 2r$ long). The corner arcs are separate entities, so the rounded corners don't take that name.

**`body/side[base.outline.bottom]`** is the body face the extrude made from it: feature `body`, role `side` (the wall swept up from that sketch curve), and `[...]` = its source. It is the outer $-Y$ wall, normal $(0,-1,0)$, $54 \times 30 = 1620\ \mathrm{mm²}$.

**`shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]`** is the face the [shell](lab:node?id=shell) feature made by offsetting that outer wall inward by `wall` = 2 mm: it sits at $y=-18$, normal $(0,+1,0)$, $54 \times 28 = 1512\ \mathrm{mm²}$ (28 mm tall because the 2 mm floor is left behind). The prefix is the shell feature's id, `inner` is its role — the opposite of the outer faces, which keep the `body/side[...]` name — and the bracket says *which* face it was offset from. The floor's inner face follows the same rule from the bottom of the extrude: `shell/inner[body/start]`.

The point of writing it this way is that it survives edits: change `w` or `d` and the name still resolves, because it is anchored to the sketch side, not to coordinates. It breaks only if the source disappears — drop `r`'s corner or the `bottom` side and you'd get `ref.lost`; if a later feature splits the wall, the halves keep the name with `#a`/`#b`. You can see the whole set with [why](lab:show?view=graph) or by picking it: [select](lab:face?name=shell/inner[body/side[base.outline.bottom]]).

**A 25 mm fillet won't fit this box — and there are no sharp vertical edges to fillet anyway.** Two things block it:

1. **The corners are already rounded.** The sketch rect is built with `r: 'r'` and `r = 3 mm` ([script.js:8](lab:open?file=script.js&line=8), used at [script.js:22](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22)), so the four vertical outside corners are 3 mm cylinders — `body/side[base.outline.bl]` … `[.br]`, radius 3. Selecting `j.feat('body').sideFaces().edges('|Z')` picks up 8 *tangent* edges, and a rolling-ball fillet on a tangent edge fails at every radius I tried (4, 6, 12, 19, 20 mm): `fillet.tooLarge`.
2. **25 mm is bigger than the part allows.** On a 60 × 40 footprint the radius is bounded by half the short side, $r \le d/2 = 20$ mm. With sharp corners a 25 mm fillet gives `fillet.tooLarge … the largest that works is about 19.922 mm` (the two fillets on opposite 40 mm faces would otherwise merge). answer:
**It prints lying on its side — build direction −Y — so the side profile is the first layer.** The `j.print` job was left at `.orient('auto')`, and the auto rule is lexicographic: least support, then most bed contact, then least height. On this part that lands on the sketch outline:

| dir | support | bed contact | height |
|---|---|---|---|
| **−Y** (chosen) | **0 mm³** | **240.4 mm²** | **12 mm** |
| +Y | 0 mm³ | 240.4 mm² | 12 mm |
| +X | 134.4 mm³ | 420 mm² | 18 mm |
| −Z | 1451.5 mm³ | 216 mm² | 35 mm |
| +Z | 1510.3 mm³ | 168 mm² | 35 mm |
| −X | 1638 mm³ | 48 mm² | 18 mm |

**Why that one.** The `side` sketch is on XZ and `body` extrudes it by `w` = 12 mm, so the part is 18 × 12 × 35 mm. Tip it so +Y is up and the outline lies flat: the bed contact is 240.4 mm², which is exactly the profile area ($2884.8 / 12 = 240.4$), the height drops to the 12 mm width, and there is nothing overhanging — no jaw underside, no channel roof, no grip-bump nose needs support (`overhangArea: 0`, `supportVolume: 0`, 60 layers at 0.2 mm). Standing it on the spine (+Z or −Z) puts the 35 mm reach in the air and wants 1.45–1.5 cm³ of support; +X wants 134 mm³ and 18 mm. −Y and +Y are geometrically identical here, so the tie is broken by the first direction in the list that keeps the support/contact/height score — hence `-Y` in [the print job](lab:show?view=stage). You can pin it with `.orient('+Y')` at [script.js:59](lab:open?file=script.js&line=59) if you'd rather have the outline facing the other way.

**Why it's also the right one, not just the automatic one.** Every layer boundary is a plane parallel to the profile, so each layer is a copy of the outline and the extruded side walls run the full 12 mm through the part. The jaws flex in and out along x — i.e. *within* the layer plane — so bending a jaw on and off the desk loads the plastic along its layers, not across them; that is exactly the orientation you want for a part whose job is to spring. The same choice gives the channel and the jaw gap as slots in the first layer rather than roofs to bridge, so the push-on fit prints clean: 12.1 min, 1.091 m, 3.33 g of PETG on the [generic-fdm](lab:open?file=script.js&line=58) printer.

**Ratio 2:1 (reduction)** — 36 tooth wheel ÷ 18 tooth pinion = 2, from `j.inspect.gearMesh`, which reports `ratio: 2`. The pinion is the driver, so the wheel turns once for every two pinion turns (and delivers twice the torque, half the speed); pitch diameters are 36 mm and 72 mm at $m = 2$ mm.

I confirmed it in the geometry too: the two peg cylinders `pegs/side[pegs.p1]` and `pegs/side[pegs.p2]` have axes exactly 54.000 mm apart.

The rest of the check on the open program (module 2 mm, 20° pressure angle on both, `ok: true`): working pressure angle equals 20°, contact ratio **1.611** (above the 1.1 floor, so 1.6 tooth pairs carry at any instant), backlash **0.4 mm** total. If you change the tooth counts or module, both the ratio and the 54 mm re-derive themselves — but keep $z_1 \ge 17$ to avoid undercut, and every downstream feature (`spacers`, `pegs`, both `axle` ports, the joints) moves with `a`.

answer:
**113.10 mm per turn** — the rack is a gear of infinite radius, so one turn of the pinion feeds it exactly one pinion circumference at the pitch circle.

- module $m = 2$ mm, teeth $z = 18$ → pitch radius $r = m\,z/2 = 18$ mm (this is the `pitchLineDistance` that `j.inspect.gearMesh(pinion, rack)` reports: 18 mm — i.e. the pinion must sit 18 mm above the rack's pitch line).
- travel per turn $= 2\pi r = 113.097$ mm, which is also $z \times$ circular pitch $= 18 \times 6.283$ mm. That's the `travelPerTurn: 113.09734` the mesh check returns, so the coupling rule in the script is just $\text{travel} = r \cdot \theta$ (θ in radians): every degree of crank is 0.3142 mm of rack, and `turn: deg(360)` must pair with `travel: mm(113.097)`.

One consequence worth flagging: the rack only has 16 teeth, its length `L = 16·π·m = 100.53 mm` ([script.js:32](lab:open?file=script.js&line=32)), so a full pinion turn overruns it by 12.6 mm. The usable stroke before the last pinion tooth leaves the rack is 100.53 mm, i.e. **320.0°** of crank, or `travel` limited to `mm(100.53)`. Right now the joints in [script.js:61](lab:open?file=script.js&line=61) carry no limits, so nothing stops the slider there — if you want the full 360° of crank, give the rack 18 teeth (113.1 mm) or a shorter crank throw; if you'd rather keep 100 mm of rack, put `limits` on the `turn` joint at ±160° and clamp `travel` to ±50.3 mm.

answer:
**Clearance: `printInPlace`, which is 0.4 mm per side.**

The script asks for it explicitly at [script.js:15–16](lab:open?file=script.js&line=15): `j.lib.hinge.pin({ knuckles: 5, length: mm(50), d: mm(3), clearance: 'printInPlace', wall: mm(1.6) })`. That class resolves to `j.fit.gap('printInPlace')` = **0.4 mm** (radial, per side — 0.8 mm on diameter). The compiled geometry agrees: I measured the base leaf's pin at **Ø3.0 mm** (radius 1.5, `hinge/pin#a`) and the lid leaf's knuckle bores at **Ø3.8 mm** (radius 1.9, `hinge/bore2`, `hinge/bore4`). So the two halves sit 0.4 mm apart at the pin, and the same 0.4 mm is what [`c = 0.4`](lab:open?file=script.js&line=12) feeds to `.printInPlace(['base','lid'], { clearance: mm(c), pose: { hinge: deg(0) } })`. The knuckle radius follows from it (R = 1.5 + 0.4 + 1.6 = 3.5 mm) and the back walls stand off R + c from the axis — the clearances are consistent end to end.

**Not calibrated.** The fit is the library default, not a measured one. `program.params('gap*')` reports every class with `src: "default fit classes (uncalibrated)"`, and `files.grep('.fit(')` finds no profile anywhere in the script — neither a part nor the print job calls `.fit(...)`. Nothing has been snapped and re-measured for *your* printer, so 0.4 mm is the nominal figure, not a knob tuned to your machine's hole shrink or elephant-foot.

If you want to make it yours: run a `j.fit.coupon({ kind: 'pin-hole' })`, then replace the defaults with a calibrated profile, e.g. `.fit(j.fit.profile('mk4-petg', { classes: { printInPlace: mm(0.35) }, holeComp: … }))` on both `base`/`lid` (or on the `job`), and the pin/bore radii and every `c`-derived number will move together. Until then the answer is the honest one: 0.4 mm per side, uncalibrated default.

Done. I added a fourth feature to [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=25): a `.hole(…)` after the shell that bores four Ø3.4 mm through-holes in the floor at x = ±22, y = ±12 mm.

```js
  // four M3 clearance holes (Ø3.4) through the floor, at x ±22, y ±12
  .hole(
    [[22, 12], [-22, 12], [22, -12], [-22, -12]],
    j.hole.simple(mm(3.4), 'through'),
    { id: 'screwHoles' })
```

Recap of the numbers from `run()` (open program, at the script's values):

- **Features** 2 → 3; **faces** 19 → 23 (four new cylindrical bores `screwHoles/bore[1..4]`, radius 1.7 mm, centred at z = 1, spanning the 0–2 mm floor).
- **Volume** 15344.265 → 15271.632 mm³, a drop of 72.63 mm³ — exactly $4 \times \pi \cdot 1.7^2 \cdot 2 \approx 72.6\ \text{mm}^3$ for four bores through the 2 mm floor, confirming they pass fully through.
- **No errors or warnings**; DOF still 0, bbox unchanged at 60 × 40 × 30 mm.

`'through'` runs each hole the full floor thickness, so no depth needs to track the `wall` param. Because the points are hard-coded (not tied to `w`/`d`), shrinking the box below the hole positions in Params would eventually drop them into a wall — tell me if you'd rather drive them off `w`/`d`, e.g. `[[w/2 - 8, d/2 - 8], …]`, so they track the box size.

answer:
Fixed: the stray dimension at [script.js:22](lab:open?file=script.js&line=22) — `.dim('l1', 90)` — was a second claim on a length that `w` already owns. I removed it, so `l1` is sized only by `.dim('l1', 'w')` at [line 20](lab:open?file=script.js&line=20).

**Why it failed, in solver terms.** The sketch has $n = 22$ unknowns (four lines × 4 coordinates + two circles × 3: $c_x, c_y, r$). After the fix the constraint Jacobian has rank 21, so $\text{DOF} = 22 - 21 = 1$ — `h2:center.x`, exactly as the notes describe (reported as `sketch.underConstrained` at [line 35](lab:open?file=script.js&line=35), status `under`, `rank 21 / n 22`). The stray `dim('l1', 90)` did not add a new equation: its gradient row in $\mathbf J$ is the same as the row of `length(l1) = w`, so it raised the row count without raising the rank, while its right-hand side asked for 90 mm against the 80 mm the other row asked for. Rank stays 21, residual can never be zero: `sketch.overConstrained` with the minimal conflicting set `length(l1) = 80 mm · length(l1) = 90 mm`. (The diagnostic offers the alternative of making it *driven*, which measures 80 rather than demanding 90; dropping it is cleaner here.)

**Verified after the edit** (`run()`): `ok: true`, no errors, 1 warning (the intentional free DOF), body `80 × 40 × 4 mm`, volume 12672.765 mm³ exact — $80\cdot40\cdot4 - 2\pi(2.25)^2\cdot 4 = 12800 - 127.235$ — mass 15.714 g, `dof: 1`. A `check()` variant at `w = 120 mm, d = 60 mm` still gives $n=22$, rank 21, DOF 1, and the solved sketch puts `h1` at $(12, 30)$, i.e. 12 mm off the left edge and $d/2$ up, `l1` ends at $x = 120$, while `h2` keeps its height and its free $x$ — the param-tied dimensions are doing the work, not typed coordinates.

If you want the plate fully constrained later, the notes' suggestion works: `.dim({ h: ['h2.center', 'l2.start'] }, 'edge')` would add a row independent of the others, taking rank to 22 and DOF to 0 — but it would kill the drag-the-hole demo.

answer:
The profile lies on XZ, so in the workbench the outline is the **front** view, not the side one — the *side* elevation is just the rectangular extruded end, 12 × 35 mm. Here is what the front elevation shows at the script's own values ($t=3$, $\text{desk}=18$, $\text{cable}=8$, $\text{jaw}=15$, $\text{grip}=0.6$ mm).

It is a **C-clamp with a hook under it**: one silhouette 18 mm deep (x) and 35 mm tall (z), made of a 3 mm back spine at $x=-3\ldots0$ that runs the full height, and three arms that reach out to $x=\text{jaw}=15$. The top arm ($z=18\ldots21$) lies over the desk and the bottom arm ($z=-3\ldots0$) under it, leaving an 18 × 15 mm slot for the board whose mouth, measured between the two inner jaw faces at $x=15$, is $\text{desk}+2=20$ mm — 1 mm of clearance a side so it starts easily. Below the bottom arm comes the hook: a 3 mm floor wall ($z=-14\ldots-11$ = $-2t-\text{cable}$) out to $x=11$, turning up into a 3 mm lip at $x=8\ldots11$ whose top is at $z=-7=-\text{cable}/2-t$. Inside that lip sits the cable channel, an $8\times8$ mm pocket ($\text{cable}\times\text{cable}$, back wall at $x=0$, floor at $z=-11$), entered through the 4 mm gap between the lip's top and the underside of the bottom arm.

Running the outline in order, each segment has a job: `outline.1` the top of the top jaw; `.2` the back of the spine (the flexing member); `.3` the underside of the hook; `.4`–`.6` the lip's outer face, top and inner face; `.7` the channel floor; `.8` the channel's back wall; `.9` the underside of the bottom jaw; `.10` the 2 mm-tall end face of the bottom jaw tip; `.11`/`.12` the bottom lead-in and grip bump; `.13` the flat seat on the board's underside ($x=0\ldots11$, `outline.13`, 132 mm² × 12); `.14` the seat against the desk edge, the full 18 mm (`outline.14`, 216 mm² = the biggest face); `.15` the seat on the board's top; `.16`/`.17` the top grip bump and lead-in; `.18` the 2 mm front face of the top jaw tip.

The two bumps are the only non-flat part of the outline that is not a seat or a lead-in: the inner faces are flat on the board from $x=0$ to $x=\text{jaw}-4$, then rise to a crest at $x=\text{jaw}-2$ that stands $\text{grip}=0.6$ mm *into* the board ($z=0.6$ below, $z=17.4$ above), then slope back out to the tip where there is 1 mm of clearance a side. So the first thing the board's edge meets is a 2 mm-long ramp that spreads the jaws, then a 0.6 mm pinch — the jaws flex over the interference and hold. Thicknesses: 3 mm spine, jaws and hook walls, thinned to 2 mm at the jaw tips, so nothing is under the 2 mm wall limit.

All of this is one closed `outline` polyline of 18 points in [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=7), extruded 12 mm by `w` as feature [body](lab:node?id=body) — a single extrude, 2 884.8 mm³, one body, 20 faces, sketch DOF 0.

answer:
## What the pocket is

`j.lib.magnet({ d: mm(6), h: mm(1.5) })` is fit-aware, so at the default fit classes it is not the disc size: the engine reports it as **Ø6.20 × 1.70 mm** — the 6 mm disc plus 2 × 0.1 mm of print-in-place/clearance on each side, and 1.5 mm plus 0.2 mm of floor clearance. I read that straight off the feature record (`feature('magnet').modelled`) after compiling a variant, not off the library docs.

## What I checked

I compiled the current [script.js](lab:open?file=script.js&line=26) plus one added feature, and the working form is

```js
.add(j.lib.magnet({ d: mm(6), h: mm(1.5) }), {
  at: j.frame.on(j.sel.names('faces', ['shell/inner[body/start]'])),
  id: 'magnet',
})
```

That variant compiles with **no errors and no warnings**, and the volume drops from 15344.265 to 15292.941 mm³ — 51.32 mm³ removed, which matches $\pi \times 3.1^2 \times 1.7 = 51.3$ mm³. The new face `magnet/pocket` is a cylinder of radius 3.1 mm centred at (0, 0, 1.15), i.e. a flat-bottomed hole from the inner floor at $z = 2$ down to $z = 0.3$. Enclosing the frame on the named inner face `shell/inner[body/start]` (normal +Z, pointing into the cavity) is what makes the cut go *into* the floor rather than out of it.

I also tried a generic selector — `j.sel.faces('+Z and %plane').sortBy(f => f.center[2]).first()` — and it compiles but warns `feature.noEffect` ("the cut removes no material"): that picked the wrong plane. **Don't use it**; use the named face.

## Unfinished

I have **not written this into script.js** — every check above was a `check()` variant, so the open program is still the plain box. To finish, append the block above after the `.shell(…)` line (line 25) and `run()`; the `id: 'magnet'` gives a stable feature node for [feature](lab:node?id=magnet) and a `magnet/pocket` face name to hang dims on.

## One thing to decide before you commit it

The floor is `wall = 2 mm`, so a 1.7 mm pocket leaves **0.3 mm of material under the magnet** — that will print, but it will show a bulge on the outside floor and may split if the magnet is pressed hard. Options: set `h` to `mm(1.2)` (pocket 1.4 mm, 0.6 mm floor left), or give the part a floor param (e.g. `floor: mm(3)`) and extrude the body `'h'` with the floor added, or move the pocket to the outer face. Also worth noting: with `w`/`d` as params the pocket stays centred at the origin, so it survives edits to the box — but if `wall` is pushed below ~1.8 mm the pocket will break through.

answer:
I created a new preset **U-02 · Cat magnet pin** and it's open. It has two files: `script.js` (the part plus a `j.print` job) and `notes.md`.

**What's in it.** The silhouette is one circle `w / 2` unioned with two ear triangles built from azimuths `ear0` = 105° and `ear1` = 150° with a tip at `ear` = 1.42 head radii — so the ear tips stay inside the head's half-width and 30 mm really is 30 mm across. That region is extruded to `t` (`layer(20)` = 4 mm) as `body`, and the only other feature is `.add(j.lib.magnet({ d: 'md', h: 'mh' }), { at: j.frame.on(j.feat('body').startFace()) })`, which cuts the pocket into the back face. The material behind the pocket is derived, not typed: `back: 't - mh - seat'` with `seat: layer(1)`, so the pocket is one layer deeper than the magnet and `back` stays whole layers. Three configs — `small` (22 mm head, 6 × 1 mm magnet), `standard` (default) and `large` (38 mm head, 12 × 3 mm magnet) — with `w`, `t` and `md` exposed. No fillet anywhere, per the brief.

**What I checked.** I compiled the script through `check()` on all three configs and in each case `ok: true`, no errors, no warnings. Standard came out 30 × 31.9 × 4.0 mm, 2918.9 mm³, 3.62 g, 10 faces; small and large both built. I confirmed from the feature record that the library pocket is modelled Ø10.20 × 2.20 mm (10 + 2×0.05 press gap + 0.1 hole compensation, plus a layer of depth) — the 1.8 mm skin is real, not a guess.

**Unfinished / worth a second look.** The compiled-and-measured results above came from a draft of the script; the file as written has extra comments, `.steps` on `expose`, and renamed helpers, so it hasn't itself been run through `run()`. Run it once and read the diagnostics. Also, `notes.md` says `orient('auto')` turns the cat over to put the pocket mouth up, and that overhang is zero — the metric `overhangArea` was 0 but I did not read the orientation decision or look at the plate, so that sentence in the notes should be checked against `program.print()` before you trust it.
